fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A system older than the ancient world", "body": "David Mathisen argues that ancient Egypt, Sumer, India, China and cultures across Africa, the Americas and the Pacific are all working from one celestial system, which means the source has to be older than any of them. He calls that source the deep ancient, separated from recorded history by a cataclysm around thirteen thousand years ago, the event pointed to by Comet Research Group work on the Younger Dryas. His 2019 book Ancient Worldwide System traces the same star patterns through Indian, Egyptian and Mesopotamian myth. The ancients inherited the system, he says, but probably no longer fully understood it."}, {"title": "Thor is the constellation Hercules", "body": "The core demonstration of the episode is that Thor is the constellation Hercules as outlined by H.A. Ray in The Stars, A New Way to See Them. Mathisen points to the same signature every time, a weapon brandished overhead, the other arm outstretched, a deep lunge with the rear heel raised, and the square keystone head that becomes a full beard. Four faint stars above that head form the axe or hammer, and one extra star shortens the handle, matching the Edda story where Loki, disguised as a fly, spoils the dwarf Brokkr's work."}, {"title": "The same thunderer in every language", "body": "Once the outline is fixed, Mathisen and Chance Garton run it around the world. Zeus appears in that exact lunge on a Greek vase in Munich, fighting Typhon, who is Ophiuchus. Shango of the Yoruba carries an axe, Chaac of the Maya takes the pose on an eighth century cup in the Met, and Indra plays the same part in India. Garton adds Sancus of the Umbrians, whom the Greeks equated with Hercules, plus Taranis of the Britons and the Phoenician word for thunder. Tacitus and Herodotus, they note, already treated these gods as equivalents."}, {"title": "Literalism as a second catastrophe", "body": "Mathisen treats literalist religion as a deliberate takeover rather than an innocent misreading, the argument of his books The Undying Stars and Myth and Trauma. He cites Michael Hudson on Hammurabi and the debt jubilees the ancient world practiced, and says the destruction of the old system is what made feudalism and oligarchy possible. Garton reads Synesius of Alexandria admitting he will preach fables in public and stay a philosopher in private. Robert Taylor, an English minister who laid all this out in the 1820s, spent three years in jail for it."}, {"title": "Ophiuchus, the world tree and the cure for trauma", "body": "The second half turns to Ophiuchus, the constellation just below Hercules, which Mathisen reads as the mountain, the tombstone, the tablets of the law, the Shiva lingam, and the spear bearer behind Odin, Moses, Athena and Solomon. Redraw Hercules as a whirling disk and it becomes a scraggly tree standing on that mountain, which is Yggdrasil, the fig tree Odysseus clings to, the rowan that saves Thor. The point, he insists, is practical. The myths exist to heal trauma in individuals and societies, and symbolic literacy is psychic self defense."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: David Warner Mathisen returns to InnerVerse to pick up where we left off two weeks ago, and take a deeper look at the universal star myths from whence we receive the legends of Ygdrassil, and the mightiest Asgardian thunder god, Thor. There will surely be more in store beyond these topics, so tune in and edify your mind!
